title: Statement on Inclusive and Sustainable Artificial Intelligence for People and the Planet
original_title: Déclaration sur une intelligence artificielle inclusive et durable pour les peuples et la planète
issuing_body: Signatories of the AI Action Summit, Paris (hosted by the French Presidency): 63 countries, the African Union Commission and the EU
summary: This summit outcome moves the emphasis from frontier safety to inclusion, sustainability, openness and the future of work. It still calls for AI that is 'human rights based, human-centric, ethical, safe, secure and trustworthy', credits the Bletchley and Seoul safety work, and commits to address AI risks to information integrity. It also backs a UN Global Dialogue on AI governance and an Independent International Scientific Panel on AI.
safety_topics: international cooperation; transparency & labelling; accountability & liability
notes: Issued after the AI Action Summit, 10-11 Feb 2025. The United States and United Kingdom did not sign. The signatory list on the Élysée page shows 65 signatories (63 countries plus the AU Commission and the EU). The International AI Safety Report 2025 was published for this summit.

title: New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact
issuing_body: Participants of the India AI Impact Summit 2026, New Delhi (hosted by the Government of India)
summary: This outcome of the fourth summit in the series is built on three 'Sutras' (People, Planet, Progress) and seven pillars, including 'secure and trusted AI'. That pillar treats security of AI systems as foundational to trust, says understanding of potential security risks needs to deepen, and notes voluntary industry measures and policy frameworks across the AI lifecycle. All deliverables are voluntary and non-binding, including a Trusted AI Commons platform for safety tools, benchmarks and best practices.
safety_topics: international cooperation; evaluation & testing; research priorities
notes: The summit's high-level segment was held in New Delhi in Feb 2026; PIB gives 18-19 Feb, while All India Radio reported on 21 Feb that it 'concluded yesterday'. The exact adoption day is unclear, so only the month is given. PIB's endorsement list, current to 5 Mar 2026, shows 92 countries and international organisations, including the USA, China and the EU; earlier reports said 88. Companion outcome documents include the Charter for the Democratic Diffusion of AI, the Framework for the Trusted AI Commons, a Guidance Note on AI Governance, 'AI and Child Safety', and the Guiding Principles on Resilient, Innovative and Efficient AI. The New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments (19 Feb 2026) are voluntary company commitments on sharing anonymised AI-usage insights and on multilingual and contextual evaluations; they contain no explicit safety-testing commitments.

title: The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit, 1-2 November 2023
issuing_body: Governments attending the AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park (28 countries and the EU), hosted by the UK Government
summary: First intergovernmental declaration focused on 'frontier AI' (highly capable general-purpose models). It warns of serious, even catastrophic, harm from misuse and loss of control, singles out cybersecurity, biotechnology and disinformation risks, and calls for shared scientific understanding, risk-based policies, safety testing and evaluation, and transparency from frontier developers.
safety_topics: general-purpose / frontier AI; catastrophic risk; evaluation & testing; transparency & labelling; international cooperation; research priorities
notes: Signed at the first AI Safety Summit, 1-2 Nov 2023. Signatories include the US, China and the EU. It launched the summit series: Seoul (May 2024), Paris (Feb 2025), New Delhi (Feb 2026). It also led to the International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI. GOV.UK shows the page as last updated 13 Feb 2025; the text itself is unchanged.

title: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law
issuing_body: Council of Europe Committee of Ministers
summary: The first legally binding international treaty on AI. Parties must ensure that activities across the AI lifecycle are consistent with human rights, democracy and the rule of law, through risk and impact assessment, transparency, oversight, accountability and remedies. It applies fully to the public sector; for the private sector, Parties choose how to address risks.
safety_topics: accountability & liability; transparency & labelling; human oversight; risk-based classification; public-sector use; international cooperation
notes: Adopted by the Committee of Ministers on 17 May 2024 and opened for signature in Vilnius on 5 Sep 2024. It enters into force on the first day of the month after a three-month period starting from the fifth ratification, of which at least three must be CoE member states. The CoE page lists 21 signatories: Albania, Andorra, Armenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Norway, Republic of Moldova, San Marino, Switzerland, Ukraine, UK, Canada, EU, Israel, Japan, USA and Uruguay. The EU ratified on 15 May 2026 at the 135th Committee of Ministers session in Chișinău. As of Oct 2026 the CoE AI page lists only the EU as a Party and no entry into force has been announced. A June 2026 CDNET report urges ratification 'with a view to achieving early entry into force'. The Steering Committee for New and Emerging Digital Technologies (CDNET), which replaced the CAI, is the treaty's custodian; first plenary 15-17 Apr 2026, second plenary 21-23 Oct 2026.

jurisdiction: International AI Safety Report (AI Safety Summit process)

issuing_body: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
summary: The world's first comprehensive horizontal AI law. notes: Adopted 13 June 2024. Published in OJ L on 12 July 2024. Entered into force 1 August 2024. Original phased application (Arts 111 and 113): 2 Feb 2025 for Chapters I–II (definitions, AI literacy, Art. 5 prohibitions 1–8); 2 Aug 2025 for GPAI model obligations (Ch. V), governance (AI Office, AI Board), notified bodies and penalties (except Art. 101 GPAI fines); 2 Aug 2026 for general application, including Art. 50 transparency, GPAI fines and the start of enforcement by the AI Office and national authorities; 2 Aug 2027 for Art. 6(1)/Annex I high-risk systems and for GPAI models placed on the market before 2 Aug 2025; 31 Dec 2030 for Annex X large-scale IT systems. AMENDED by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI), in force 27 July 2026: Annex III (stand-alone) high-risk obligations moved from 2 Aug 2026 to 2 Dec 2027; Annex I (product-embedded) high-risk obligations moved from 2 Aug 2027 to 2 Aug 2028; a new Art. 5 prohibition (AI systems generating non-consensual sexual/intimate content or CSAM) applies from 2 Dec 2026; the Art. 50(2) marking grace period for generative systems already on the market ends 2 Dec 2026; the deadline for national regulatory sandboxes is 2 Aug 2027; the Art. 4 AI-literacy duty is simplified. summary: Template required under AI Act Art. 53(1)(d) that sets a 'common minimal baseline' for the public summary of content used to train a GPAI model. It supports transparency and the exercise of copyright and other rights.
safety_topics: general-purpose / frontier AI; transparency & labelling
notes: Published 24 July 2025. Using the template is mandatory in the sense that Art. 53(1)(d) requires the summary to follow the AI Office template. Last updated 26 March 2026.
verification_note: The Commission library page confirmed the title, publication date of 24 July 2025 and last update of 26 March 2026.

title: Draft guidance and reporting template on serious AI incidents (Article 73 AI Act)
issuing_body: European Commission (AI Office)
summary: Draft Commission guidance and a template for high-risk AI providers' duty under Art. 73 to report serious incidents to national market-surveillance authorities. It clarifies definitions, gives examples, explains the interplay with other reporting regimes, and aligns with the OECD AI Incidents Monitor and Common Reporting Framework.
safety_topics: incident reporting; general-purpose / frontier AI; accountability & liability
notes: Draft published for consultation on 26 Sept 2025; the consultation closed 7 Nov 2025. Art. 73(7) required the guidance by 2 Aug 2025. A final version of the high-risk guidance was not found as of 11 Oct 2026; a Commission page lists a 'Template for reporting serious incidents by providers of high-risk AI systems' as published, but without a date. Separately, a final reporting template for serious incidents involving GPAI models with systemic risk (Art. 55; GPAI Code Commitment 9) was published on 4 Nov 2025. Art. 73 obligations follow the high-risk application dates, as revised by the Digital Omnibus.
verification_note: The Commission consultation page confirmed the draft status, publication on 26 Sept 2025 and the 7 Nov 2025 deadline. The Commission library page confirmed the GPAI serious-incident template of 4 Nov 2025. Final high-risk guidance could not be confirmed (web search budget was exhausted before a final check).

title: Draft Commission guidelines on the classification of high-risk AI systems
issuing_body: European Commission (AI Office)
summary: Draft guidelines under AI Act Art. 6(5) on classifying AI systems as high-risk, both as safety components of Annex I products and as Annex III use cases. They cover the Art. 6(3) filter for systems that do not pose a significant risk, with practical examples. The draft was published for targeted stakeholder consultation.
safety_topics: risk-based classification; critical infrastructure; public-sector use
notes: The AI Act required these guidelines by 2 Feb 2026, but they were delayed. A draft was published on 19 May 2026 for targeted consultation, and the page was last updated 23 July 2026. No final version was found as of 11 Oct 2026. Their urgency eased after the Digital Omnibus moved Annex III obligations to 2 Dec 2027 and Annex I obligations to 2 Aug 2028.
verification_note: The Commission library page confirmed the title, draft status, publication date of 19 May 2026 and last update of 23 July 2026. COM(2026) 234 (20 May 2026) confirmed the guidelines were still in preparation. No final version was found.

title: Report from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council on the need to review the list of prohibited AI practices and of high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III
issuing_body: European Commission
summary: The first annual assessment required by AI Act Art. 112(1). It concludes there is no immediate need to amend the Art. 5 prohibitions or the Annex III high-risk list because implementation experience is limited. It flags AI-generated child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate deepfakes as a possible regulatory gap to monitor.
safety_topics: prohibited practices; risk-based classification; deepfakes & synthetic media; child safety
notes: Adopted 20 May 2026. The gap it identified (CSAM and non-consensual intimate deepfakes) was addressed in parallel by the new Art. 5 prohibition in the Digital Omnibus on AI (agreed 7 May 2026; applies from 2 Dec 2026). The report also notes that national competent authorities were still being designated and that high-risk classification guidelines were still in preparation.
verification_note: The EUR-Lex HTML of COM(2026) 234 final loaded and confirmed the title, date (Brussels, 20 May 2026), Art. 112(1) basis and conclusions.

title: Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content
short_title: Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content
issuing_body: European Commission (AI Office), drafted by independent chairs; assessed as adequate by the Commission and the AI Board
summary: A voluntary code that helps providers and deployers of generative AI meet AI Act Art. 50(2), (4) and (5). Section 1 covers providers' machine-readable marking and detection of AI-generated or manipulated content. Section 2 covers deployers' labelling of deepfakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest, supported by EU icons for labelling.
safety_topics: transparency & labelling; deepfakes & synthetic media
notes: Drafting began with a kick-off plenary on 5 Nov 2025. First draft 17 Dec 2025. Second draft 3 Mar 2026. Final code published 10 June 2026. On 8 July 2026 the Commission concluded that it adequately covers Art. 50(2), (4) and (5); the opinion was published 9 July 2026 and the AI Board adopted its adequacy assessment the following day. About 190 organisations had signed by end of July 2026. Adherence does not conclusively prove compliance.
verification_note: The Commission policy page confirmed the two sections, the drafting timeline (final code 10 June 2026) and about 190 signatories. The Commission news item of 10 June 2026 confirmed publication. The Commission opinion page confirmed the assessment concluded on 8 July 2026.

title: Action Plan on Cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence
short_title: EU Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI
issuing_body: European Commission
summary: A Commission Communication on the risks advanced AI poses for cybersecurity, such as automated attacks and vulnerability discovery at scale. Actions include building an EU third-party evaluation capacity for advanced AI model capabilities and risks in support of the AI Office, an ENISA blueprint for structured access to advanced AI for cyber defence, and a secure testing platform with the JRC for critical sectors. It also covers stronger NIS2 and Cyber Resilience Act implementation.
safety_topics: general-purpose / frontier AI; evaluation & testing; critical infrastructure; national security & military
notes: Adopted 7 July 2026 in Strasbourg. Included because its main focus is risks from advanced AI and pre-market model evaluation, which is safety content, not industrial policy. By contrast, the AI Continent Action Plan (COM(2025) 165, 9 Apr 2025) and the Apply AI Strategy (COM(2025) 723, Oct 2025) were reviewed and excluded as primarily adoption, investment and competitiveness strategies with only high-level references to trustworthy or safe AI.
verification_note: The Commission library page confirmed the title, date of 7 July 2026 and objectives. The Commission news page of 7 July 2026 confirmed the key actions (evaluation capacity, ENISA blueprint, testing platform). Council document ST-11711-2026-INIT confirmed the reference COM(2026) 577 final, dated 7 July 2026.

title: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 July 2026 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)
issuing_body: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
summary: Targeted amendment to the AI Act. It postpones high-risk obligations to fixed dates (2 Dec 2027 for Annex III, 2 Aug 2028 for Annex I) and adds a new prohibition on AI systems that generate non-consensual sexual or intimate content or child sexual abuse material. It also shortens the grace period for marking AI-generated content, strengthens AI Office supervision of AI systems built on GPAI models and of AI embedded in very large online platforms and search engines, and extends SME simplifications to small mid-caps.
safety_topics: risk-based classification; prohibited practices; general-purpose / frontier AI; transparency & labelling; deepfakes & synthetic media; child safety
notes: Commission proposal COM(2025) 836 of 19 Nov 2025, part of the Digital Omnibus/simplification package. As proposed, high-risk application would have been tied to the availability of standards and support tools, with a maximum delay of 16 months. Council general approach 13 Mar 2026. Provisional trilogue agreement 7 May 2026. Coreper endorsement 13 May 2026. EP plenary vote 16 Jun 2026 (423–57–174). Council final adoption 29 Jun 2026. Signed 8 Jul 2026. Published in OJ L 24 Jul 2026 (from secondary reporting, consistent with entry into force on the third day after publication). In force 27 Jul 2026. Key dates: 2 Aug 2026, general AI Act application incl. Art. 50 and AI Office powers (Arts 75, 75a–75d); 2 Dec 2026, new Art. 5 prohibition, and Art. 50(2) marking deadline for generative systems placed on the market before 2 Aug 2026 (grace period cut from 6 to 3 months); 2 Aug 2027, at least one national sandbox per Member State; 2 Dec 2027, Annex III high-risk; 2 Aug 2028, Annex I high-risk. It also reinstates (simplified) EU-database registration for systems claimed exempt under Art. 6(3), and allows processing of special-category data for bias detection only where strictly necessary. The AI Office's supervision of GPAI-based systems excludes uses such as law enforcement, border management, judicial authorities and financial institutions. Machinery is exempted from direct applicability, with delegated acts for health and safety requirements. Also amends Regulations (EU) 2018/1139 (aviation safety) and (EU) 2023/1230 (machinery). The separate horizontal Digital Omnibus (data/GDPR) is not AI-specific and is not recorded here.
verification_note: EUR-Lex ELI page loaded and confirmed the title, act date of 8 July 2026, and first entry-into-force date of 27 July 2026 (metadata). Council press releases of 7 May 2026 (agreement) and 29 June 2026 (final adoption) confirmed the content and dates. The Commission news item 'AI Omnibus enters into force' (27 July 2026) confirmed the 2 Dec 2027 and 2 Aug 2028 dates. The EP Legislative Train confirmed COM(2025) 836, 19 Nov 2025, 2025/0359(COD) and the plenary vote of 16 June 2026.

title: Guidelines on the implementation of the transparency obligations for certain AI systems under Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the 'AI Act')
issuing_body: European Commission
summary: Non-binding Commission guidelines on the Art. 50 duties, which apply from 2 Aug 2026. They cover disclosure that a user is interacting with an AI system, machine-readable marking and detectability of AI-generated or manipulated content, notice of emotion recognition and biometric categorisation, labelling of deepfakes and AI-generated public-interest text, and horizontal accessibility requirements.
safety_topics: transparency & labelling; deepfakes & synthetic media
notes: Draft guidelines were published for consultation on 8 May 2026. The final guidelines were annexed to a Commission Communication approving their content, C(2026) 5054 final of 20 July 2026. They complement the Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content. Under the Digital Omnibus, generative systems placed on the market before 2 Aug 2026 have until 2 Dec 2026 to meet Art. 50(2) marking.
verification_note: The Commission news page confirmed publication on 20 July 2026 and the content. The official PDF on the AI Act Service Desk confirmed the exact title and the C(2026) 5054 final reference dated 20.7.2026.

title: Policy for the responsible use of AI in government
issuing_body: Digital Transformation Agency (DTA)
summary: Mandatory whole-of-government policy for non-corporate Commonwealth entities using AI. Agencies must appoint accountable officials (by 30 Nov 2024) and publish AI transparency statements (by 28 Feb 2025). The policy aims to make government an exemplar of safe and responsible AI use.
safety_topics: public-sector use; accountability & liability; transparency & labelling
notes: Took effect on 1 Sep 2024. It is administratively binding on non-corporate Commonwealth entities (with some exceptions), not legislation. The DTA page fetched on 2026-10-11 still shows 'Version 1.1'.

issuing_body: Parliament of Australia
summary: Amends the Criminal Code Act 1995 to criminalise sharing non-consensual sexually explicit material online, including material created or altered using AI or other technology (deepfakes), with aggravated offences.
safety_topics: deepfakes & synthetic media; child safety

title: Voluntary AI Safety Standard
issuing_body: Department of Industry, Science and Resources – National Artificial Intelligence Centre
summary: Set 10 voluntary guardrails for organisations across the AI supply chain, covering accountability, risk management, data governance, testing, human oversight, transparency, contestability and record-keeping. It described what developers and deployers should do to use AI safely and was aligned with international standards.
safety_topics: accountability & liability; evaluation & testing; human oversight; transparency & labelling
notes: Published on 5 Sep 2024 together with the proposals paper on mandatory guardrails. On 21 Oct 2025 it was replaced by the 'Guidance for AI Adoption', which condensed the 10 guardrails into 6 essential practices. The DISR page marks it as the superseded first version.
verification_note: DISR publication page fetched: title, 5 Sep 2024 date, 10 guardrails, and replacement by the Guidance for AI Adoption on 21 Oct 2025 confirmed.

title: Introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings: proposals paper
issuing_body: Department of Industry, Science and Resources
summary: Consultation paper proposing mandatory guardrails for developing and deploying AI in high-risk settings. It sought views on the guardrails, on principles for defining high-risk AI (including general-purpose models), and on regulatory options for making the guardrails mandatory.
safety_topics: risk-based classification; general-purpose / frontier AI; accountability & liability; evaluation & testing; human oversight; transparency & labelling
notes: Consultation ran 5 Sep-4 Oct 2024. The government has since said it 'will not proceed at this time' with mandatory AI guardrails. Feedback informed the National AI Plan (released 2 Dec 2025), which relies on existing laws, regulators and the new AI Safety Institute rather than a standalone AI Act. Status is recorded as withdrawn (proposal not pursued). date_last_updated uses the National AI Plan release date as the date of the decision.

title: Guidance for AI Adoption
issuing_body: Department of Industry, Science and Resources – National Artificial Intelligence Centre
summary: Australia's current voluntary AI governance guidance for industry. It sets out six essential practices for responsible AI governance and adoption, based on Australia's AI Ethics Principles and international standards. It comes in two versions: Foundations for organisations starting out and Implementation Practices for organisations scaling up. Supporting tools include an AI screening tool, a policy template and an AI register template.
safety_topics: accountability & liability; evaluation & testing; human oversight; transparency & labelling
notes: Replaced the Voluntary AI Safety Standard (Sep 2024) by streamlining its 10 guardrails into 6 practices.
verification_note: DISR page fetched: title, 21 Oct 2025 date, six essential practices, the two versions and the relationship to the VAISS confirmed.

title: National AI Plan
issuing_body: Australian Government (Department of Industry, Science and Resources)
summary: Australia's flagship AI policy, built on three goals with three pillars each. On safety, it takes a practical, risk-based approach that relies on existing technology-neutral laws and regulators instead of mandatory AI-specific guardrails or a standalone AI Act. It funds an Australian AI Safety Institute to monitor and test frontier AI and advise government.
safety_topics: safety institute; general-purpose / frontier AI; evaluation & testing; international cooperation
notes: Released on 2 Dec 2025, according to the Government's 1 Apr 2026 response to the Senate Select Committee on Adopting AI. That decision replaced the earlier plan for mandatory guardrails for high-risk AI. Related measures cited in the response: a committed but not yet legislated Digital Duty of Care; a planned legislative framework for automated decision-making in government; Privacy Act disclosure of substantially automated decisions from 10 Dec 2026 (Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024); and the 2024 deepfake sexual material offences. Later DISR MoUs with Anthropic (1 Apr 2026) and Microsoft (23 Apr 2026) cite the Plan.

title: Australian AI Safety Institute (establishment)
issuing_body: Australian Government (Department of Industry, Science and Resources)
summary: Sets up an Australian AI Safety Institute to monitor, test and share information about emerging AI capabilities and risks. It will advise ministers, agencies and regulators, test frontier AI models, act as a hub for coordinated government action and support Australia's international AI safety commitments. It is explicitly not a regulator and complements existing laws.
safety_topics: safety institute; general-purpose / frontier AI; evaluation & testing; international cooperation
notes: Funding: A$29.8 million over four years from 2025-26, then A$7.9 million a year ongoing from 2029-30 (per the Senate committee response). The DISR news page is dated 25 November 2025 and states that the minister announced the Australian AI Safety Institute on that day, shortly before the National AI Plan; the page also carries an 'Updated 17 December' note on the renaming of the International Network of AI Safety Institutes to the 'International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science'. A DISR MoU with Canada on AI safety institute collaboration was published on 5 Mar 2026.

title: Bill No. 2338/2023 on the development, promotion and ethical and responsible use of artificial intelligence

title: Superior Electoral Court Resolution No. 23,732 of 27 February 2024 (amending Resolution 23,610/2019 on electoral propaganda: AI and synthetic content rules)
original_title: Resolução nº 23.732, de 27 de fevereiro de 2024 (altera a Res.-TSE nº 23.610/2019)
issuing_body: Superior Electoral Court (Tribunal Superior Eleitoral, TSE)
summary: Requires explicit labelling of AI-generated synthetic content in election advertising, bans deepfakes of real, deceased or fictitious persons used to harm or favour candidates (even with consent), bars chatbots or avatars that simulate conversation with candidates, and makes platforms jointly liable if they fail to remove non-compliant AI content; violations can lead to loss of registration or mandate.
safety_topics: deepfakes & synthetic media; transparency & labelling; accountability & liability
notes: Signed 27 Feb 2024; published in DJE-TSE no. 29 of 4 Mar 2024; applied to the 2024 municipal elections.

title: Directive on Automated Decision-Making
issuing_body: Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat
summary: Mandatory Treasury Board policy instrument requiring federal institutions that use automated decision systems for administrative decisions to complete an Algorithmic Impact Assessment and apply risk-tiered safeguards: notice and explanation, peer review, testing and monitoring for bias and quality, human intervention for higher-impact decisions, and recourse.
safety_topics: public-sector use; risk-based classification; human oversight; transparency & labelling; evaluation & testing; accountability & liability
notes: Binding on federal institutions as Treasury Board policy (not a statute). Launched 4 March 2019; effective April 2019, with compliance required for new systems from 1 April 2020. Amended 1 April 2021, 25 April 2023 (third review) and 24 June 2025 (fourth review: more transparency, stronger testing/monitoring and senior-level accountability; Algorithmic Impact Assessment updated). Reviewed every two years.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Part 3 of Bill C-27, Digital Charter Implementation Act, 2022)
issuing_body: Parliament of Canada (Government bill sponsored by the Minister of Innovation, Science and Industry)
summary: Would have created Canada's first federal AI statute, imposing risk-based obligations on 'high-impact' AI systems (risk assessment and mitigation, monitoring, record-keeping, transparency, notification of material harm), an AI and Data Commissioner, and offences for deploying AI that causes serious harm. It never passed committee stage and died when Parliament was prorogued.
safety_topics: risk-based classification; general-purpose / frontier AI; transparency & labelling; incident reporting; accountability & liability
notes: Introduced 16 June 2022 (first reading); referred to the Standing Committee on Industry and Technology 24 April 2023; last committee meeting 26 Sept 2024; died on the Order Paper when the 1st Session of the 44th Parliament was prorogued on 6 Jan 2025. No AIDA successor as of Oct 2026: the June 2026 National AI Strategy relies on privacy and online-safety law modernisation instead. Bill C-36 (Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, first reading 15 June 2026, sponsored by the Minister of AI and Digital Innovation) re-enacts only the privacy part of C-27 (incl. automated-decision-system disclosure) and is excluded here as a general privacy law. AI Minister Evan Solomon said in late Sept 2026 that AI deployment needs regulation but gave no details (press report, not an official source).

summary: Government-wide strategy for responsible AI adoption in federal institutions: lifecycle governance and risk frameworks proportionate to impact, ethics review of higher-risk projects with controls including emergency shutdown, security and reliability controls, an AI Centre of Expertise, and public transparency through a Government of Canada AI Register.

title: Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy: AI for All
short_title: Canada National AI Strategy (AI for All)
issuing_body: Government of Canada – Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation / Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada

title: Interim Measures for the Administration of Anthropomorphic AI Interaction Services
original_title: 人工智能拟人化互动服务管理暂行办法
issuing_body: Cyberspace Administration of China; National Development and Reform Commission; Ministry of Industry and Information Technology; Ministry of Public Security; State Administration for Market Regulation
summary: Regulates AI services that simulate human personality and give ongoing emotional companionship (32 articles). It bans virtual partner or relative services for minors, requires guardian consent for under-14s and a minor mode, and requires clear disclosure that the user is talking to AI. Other duties include reminders after every 2 hours of continuous use, measures against emotional dependence, crisis intervention for self-harm risk, easy exit, and limits on using sensitive chat data for training. Security assessments are required at launch, after major changes, and at 1 million registered or 100,000 monthly active users, and algorithms must be filed.

notes: The draft for comment was released 27 Dec 2025. Penalties range from warnings to service suspension and fines of RMB 10,000–100,000, or RMB 100,000–200,000 where harm to life or health occurs. It also calls for an AI sandbox safety service platform. Task-oriented tools without ongoing emotional interaction, such as customer service bots, are excluded.

summary: Comprehensive federal AI order that used Defense Production Act authority to require developers of dual-use foundation models above a compute threshold to report red-team safety test results to the government, tasked NIST with AI safety standards and evaluation guidance, and directed agency action on synthetic content, critical infrastructure, biosecurity and federal AI use.

notes: Signed 30 Oct 2023; published in the Federal Register 1 Nov 2023. Revoked on 20 Jan 2025 by EO 14148 (Initial Rescissions of Harmful Executive Orders and Actions). EO 14179 (23 Jan 2025) then ordered agencies to review, suspend, revise or rescind actions taken under EO 14110. Its implementing instruments (OMB M-24-10, M-24-18, NSM-25, the US AI Safety Institute) were later rescinded, replaced or reorganised.

title: Memorandum on Advancing the United States' Leadership in Artificial Intelligence; Harnessing Artificial Intelligence to Fulfill National Security Objectives; and Fostering the Safety, Security, and Trustworthiness of Artificial Intelligence (NSM-25), with the Framework to Advance AI Governance and Risk Management in National Security
issuing_body: The White House (President Joseph R. Biden Jr.) / National Security Council
summary: First national security memorandum on AI. It directs national security agencies to adopt frontier AI while managing its risks, designates the AI Safety Institute as industry's primary government point of contact, sets up classified and unclassified testing partnerships with national security agencies, and is paired with a Framework that sets prohibited and high-impact AI uses plus risk-management, evaluation and accountability requirements for national-security AI.
safety_topics: national security & military; evaluation & testing; safety institute; general-purpose / frontier AI; human oversight; public-sector use
notes: Rescinded and replaced on 5 June 2026 by National Security Presidential Memorandum 11 (NSPM-11) on AI in the national security enterprise. Because it was issued under the revoked EO 14110, it falls within the EO 14179 Sec. 5 review of EO 14110 actions, and its AISI-centred provisions are outdated by the 2025 reorganisation of AISI into CAISI. title: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust (OMB Memorandum M-25-21)
issuing_body: Office of Management and Budget, Executive Office of the President
summary: Replaces M-24-10 as the government-wide policy on agency AI use. For such AI it requires minimum practices: pre-deployment testing, AI impact assessments with independent review, ongoing monitoring, operator training, human oversight and fail-safes, and human review and appeal. Non-compliant uses must be discontinued, waivers require CAIO certification, and Chief AI Officers and governance boards remain.

issuing_body: The White House (Office of Science and Technology Policy; Special Advisor for AI and Crypto; National Security Advisor)

title: Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government (Executive Order 14319)
issuing_body: The White House (President Donald J. Trump)

OMB must issue implementing guidance that lets vendors show compliance through disclosures (such as system prompts and evaluations) instead of model weights, with exceptions for national security systems.
safety_topics: public-sector use; transparency & labelling
notes: Signed 23 Jul 2025 alongside America's AI Action Plan; published in the Federal Register 28 Jul 2025. Implemented by OMB M-26-04 (11 Dec 2025). Included because it sets binding governance requirements for federal procurement of AI models.

title: Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (Executive Order 14365)
issuing_body: The White House (President Donald J. Trump)
summary: Seeks a 'minimally burdensome' national AI standard and targets state AI laws. It creates a DOJ AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state laws and has Commerce identify 'onerous' state AI laws. It conditions BEAD non-deployment funds and other discretionary grants on state AI policy, directs an FCC proceeding on a preemptive federal reporting and disclosure standard, and requires an FTC policy statement on when state laws that force changes to truthful AI outputs are preempted. It also calls for preemptive federal legislation that spares state child-safety, AI infrastructure and state-procurement laws.
safety_topics: transparency & labelling; child safety; accountability & liability
related_ids: US-22; US-24; US-CO-01; US-CA-05; US-NY-01; US-25
notes: Signed 11 Dec 2025; published 16 Dec 2025. Implementation: (1) The AG memo of 9 Jan 2026 established the AI Litigation Task Force. Colo.); Colorado's AG agreed to a stipulated order pausing enforcement (27 Apr 2026), and Colorado repealed and replaced the law in May 2026. title: National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence: Legislative Recommendations
short_title: White House National AI Legislative Framework
issuing_body: The White House
summary: Legislative recommendations under EO 14365 Sec. 8. Congress would preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens or regulate AI development, while preserving generally applicable state laws (child protection, fraud, consumer protection), zoning for AI infrastructure, and states' own AI use. Proposes child-safety duties for AI platforms likely to be used by minors (age assurance, parental tools, self-harm and exploitation safeguards) and asks national security agencies to build capacity to understand frontier-model capabilities and risks. Creates no dedicated frontier-model regulatory regime.
safety_topics: child safety; general-purpose / frontier AI; national security & military; deepfakes & synthetic media
notes: Released 20 Mar 2026 (the date in the PDF filename, confirmed by multiple law-firm summaries). The White House fact sheet of 29 Sep 2026 calls it the 'March 2026 National Super Intelligence Policy Framework', reflecting the renaming under EO 14434. As of Oct 2026 Congress had not enacted it.

title: Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security (Executive Order 14409)
issuing_body: The White House (President Donald J. Trump)
summary: Treasury, the Department of War (through NSA) and DHS (through CISA) must create a classified benchmarking process for AI models' advanced cyber capabilities, with the NSA Director designating 'covered frontier models'. They must also design a voluntary framework under which developers can give the government access to such models for up to 30 days before release to other trusted partners. The order rules out any mandatory licensing or preclearance. It also directs CISA Binding Operational Directives, a Treasury-led voluntary AI cybersecurity clearinghouse, and DOJ prioritisation of prosecutions for AI-enabled hacking.
safety_topics: general-purpose / frontier AI; evaluation & testing; national security & military; critical infrastructure
notes: Signed 2 Jun 2026; published in the Federal Register 5 Jun 2026. Deadlines: Sec. 2(a)-(e) within 30 days (about 2 Jul 2026); Sec. 2(f) and Sec. 3 frontier-model framework within 60 days (about 1 Aug 2026). Implementation status of the voluntary pre-release access framework could not be verified. CAISI is not named; NIST/Commerce are consulted. Revokes nothing. This is the first post-2025 federal instrument with frontier-model safety-testing content; it remains voluntary.

short_title: FTC Proposed AI Accuracy Policy Statement

It argues that state laws requiring such steering, citing Colorado's AI Act, may be subject to implied conflict preemption.

title: Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act (FRONTIER Act)
issuing_body: U.S. House of Representatives (Reps. Jay Obernolte, Lori Trahan, Scott Franklin, Scott Peters, Erin Houchin, Suhas Subramanyam)
summary: Bipartisan federal frontier-AI bill covering models trained on more than 10^26 operations. Large and very large developers (tiered by revenue and AI R&D spend) would publish frontier AI frameworks, register, undergo annual independent audits, report critical safety incidents, and for the largest tier retain a licensed independent verification organisation. A new Under Secretary of Commerce for AI Security would administer it. The Commerce Secretary would gain emergency power to suspend models posing imminent catastrophic risk, and new state obligations on catastrophic-risk transparency, auditing and incident reporting would be preempted.
safety_topics: general-purpose / frontier AI; evaluation & testing; incident reporting; transparency & labelling; catastrophic risk; accountability & liability
notes: Introduced 23 Jul 2026; the House bill number could not be confirmed (congress.gov blocked). The section-by-section says preemption targets state frontier-safety laws such as CA SB 53, NY RAISE and 'IL SB-315', while saving generally applicable, deployment-based, child-protection and procurement laws. Penalties up to $1M per violation per day, and $10M per day for emergency-order violations. On 4 Jun 2026 the same lead sponsors released the broader 'Great American AI Act' discussion draft (a three-year freeze on state AI development rules, CAISI codification); per secondary sources it had not been formally introduced as of Sep 2026. On 1 Oct 2026 the sponsors welcomed the White House Accord and urged that it be codified through this bill. No committee action verified.
verification_note: Fetched the official House member press release (23 Jul 2026) and the linked section-by-section PDF, and confirmed the full title, sponsors, introduction date and provisions. Bill number not found.

title: Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence (Executive Order 14434)
issuing_body: The White House (President Donald J. Trump)
summary: Directs the executive branch to use 'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in non-statutory documents and communications, defining SI by reference to the statutory AI definition (15 U.S.C. 9401(3)). The Assistant to the President for Science and Technology must propose legislative language for a federal SI definition and conforming amendments within 60 days. The order contains no substantive safety requirements.
safety_topics: general-purpose / frontier AI
notes: Signed 29 Sep 2026; published 2 Oct 2026. It does not require changes to existing regulations, contracts or prior presidential actions. title: Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315)
issuing_body: Illinois General Assembly; signed into law by Governor JB Pritzker
official_identifier: SB 315 (104th General Assembly); Public Act number not confirmed
summary: Illinois' frontier-model safety law, signed on 6 July 2026 and effective 1 January 2027. It also creates confidential reporting channels and whistleblower protections for employees who raise AI safety concerns. Law-firm summaries describe the covered 'large frontier developers' as companies with annual gross revenue above USD 500 million that train models with more than 10^26 operations.

title: Guide to Egypt's National AI Governance Framework

summary: Policy guide for Egypt's National AI Governance Framework, approved for publication in March 2026. title: National Security Presidential Memorandum 11: Artificial Intelligence in the National Security Enterprise
short_title: NSPM-11 on AI in the national security enterprise (2026)

summary: Presidential memorandum that rescinds and replaces NSM-25 of October 2024 and sets the policy for AI across the national security enterprise under four pillars: adoption (removing barriers and bringing frontier models to national security users quickly), adaptation (commercial and open-source models from diverse suppliers), assurance (AI that is reliable, robust, steerable and controllable, with no vendor or adversary able to disable or alter fielded systems without government approval, backed by testing, evaluation, validation and verification) and accountability (no use of AI for censorship, ideological bias or unlawful surveillance; leaders answerable for civil liberties and privacy).
